# Running Simulations

[Back to Home](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/index.md)

`Simulation` runs a built `Model` in the Rust engine and returns its outputs: one series per compartment and per accumulator, with the positions on the axis they were read at. This page covers running a model, reading and aggregating its outputs, running it in continuous time as differential equations, and plotting them.

## Quick path

```python
from commol import Aggregate, ModelBuilder, Simulation

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Basic Model")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_accumulator(id="cum_ab", name="Total moved from A to B")
    .add_transition(
        id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total", accumulators=["cum_ab"]
    )
    .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 900, "B": 100, "C": 0},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=100)

print(simulation.simulation_outputs)  # ['A', 'B', 'C', 'cum_ab']
print(f"C at step 100: {results['C'][-1]:.0f}")
```

## `Simulation`

| Member                                           | Returns                | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Simulation(model)`                              | —                      | Builds the engine for the model. A model with uncalibrated parameters can be built, but not run.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `run(num_steps, *, seed=None)`                   | `SimulationResults`    | Runs from the initial state, with the model as it is now, and reports at the positions `0, 1, …, num_steps`. Raises `ValueError` if a parameter is still `None`, `InfeasibleStateError` if a difference step leaves an amount below zero ([Amounts below zero](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/transitions/#amounts-below-zero)), and `RuntimeError` that names the flow and the position if a rate is not a number. |
| `run_at(at, *, seed=None)`                       | `SimulationResults`    | Runs from the initial state and reports at the given sorted positions only. The engine decides which positions its model type accepts: a `DifferentialEquations` model any non-negative position, such as `0.5`; a `DifferenceEquations` model only integer steps. Otherwise `ValueError`, with the engine's message. See [Differential equations](#differential-equations).                                                     |
| `replicates(n, *, seed=None)`                    | `ReplicateRuns`        | For a stochastic engine: an object whose `run` and `run_at` return `SimulationReplicates`, `n` runs with one seed each. See [Randomness, seeds and replicates](#randomness-seeds-and-replicates).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `is_stochastic`                                  | `bool`                 | Whether the engine draws random numbers.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `simulation_outputs`                             | `list[str]`            | The output names, in engine order: compartments first, then accumulators.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `outputs_for(id)`                                | `list[str]`            | The outputs of one bin or accumulator.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `group_outputs(ids)`                             | `dict[str, list[str]]` | The outputs of several bins or accumulators, keyed by id.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `total_series(results, ids)`                     | `list[float]`          | The sum of all outputs of the given ids, at each position of the results.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `windowed_totals(results, ids, window, at=None)` | `list[float]`          | What the given accumulators gained in each window.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `engine`                                         | engine                 | The underlying Rust engine, for the model as it is now: the engine `model.engine.type` names (`engine.engine_type`). `engine.step()` advances it one step; `engine.reset()` returns it to the initial state.                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

Every `run` starts again from the initial state, so two calls with the same model give the same result (`Simulation.run` resets the engine first). To continue a run step by step, use the engine:

```python
first = simulation.run(num_steps=10)
again = simulation.run(num_steps=10)
print(again["A"] == first["A"])  # True: it started again

simulation.engine.step()  # step 11, from where the last run stopped
print(simulation.engine.state[0] < first["A"][-1])  # True: A keeps falling
```

The engine follows the model. When the model changed after the `Simulation` was created, for example with `update_parameters` or `apply_calibration_parameters`, `run` and `engine` rebuild the engine from the model as it is now (`Simulation._sync_engine` compares `model_dump_json()` with the JSON the engine was built from):

```python
model.update_parameters({"k1": 0.0})
frozen = simulation.run(num_steps=10)
print(frozen["A"][10] == frozen["A"][0])  # True: k1 = 0 stops A → B
model.update_parameters({"k1": 0.3})
```

## Results

`run` and `run_at` return `SimulationResults` (`py-commol/commol/api/results.py`): a `dict` from output name to one value per position, so `results["A"]`, `json.dumps(results)` and `pandas.DataFrame(results)` work as for any mapping. The positions the values were read at are in `results.positions`.

| Member              | Shape                                                                 | Use for                                         |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `results[name]`     | `[value at positions[0], …]`                                          | Reading one output, plotting                    |
| `results.positions` | `[0.0, 1.0, …, n]` for `run(n)`; the requested positions for `run_at` | Reading a value at a position, windows, reports |
| `results.rows()`    | `[[every output at positions[0]], …]`, in `simulation_outputs` order  | Matrix operations, export                       |

`run(num_steps)` holds `num_steps + 1` positions: position 0 is the initial state.

```python
rows = results.rows()

print(results.positions[:3])  # [0.0, 1.0, 2.0]
print(len(rows))              # 101
print(len(rows[0]))           # 4: A, B, C and cum_ab
print([round(value) for value in rows[0]])  # [900, 100, 0, 0]
```

## Randomness, seeds and replicates

A stochastic engine draws random numbers, so its runs depend on a seed; a deterministic engine, such as `DifferenceEquations` and `DifferentialEquations`, gives the same run for every seed (`EngineType.is_stochastic` in `crates/commol-core/src/types/engine.rs`).

| Call                                   | Deterministic engine                                                      | Stochastic engine                                                                                 |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `run(n, seed=s)`, `run_at(at, seed=s)` | Ignores the seed; `results.seed` is `None`                                | One run from seed `s`; `results.seed` is `s`                                                      |
| `run(n)` without a seed                | `results.seed` is `None`                                                  | Draws a seed from the operating system and keeps it in `results.seed`, so the run can be repeated |
| `replicates(n, seed=s).run(…)`         | Raises `ValueError` that names the engine: every replicate would be equal | `n` runs, in parallel in the engine, each with its own seed                                       |

```python
print(simulation.is_stochastic)                # False: a difference engine
print(simulation.run(num_steps=5, seed=1).seed)  # None: the run depends on no seed
try:
    simulation.replicates(10)
except ValueError as error:
    print(error)  # The DifferenceEquations engine is deterministic: ...
```

Replicate `i` takes the seed derived from `seed` and `i`, the SplitMix64 of `seed + i` (`replicate_seed` in `crates/commol-random/src/generator.rs`), so a replicate gives the same run however many replicates run, and `simulation.run(…, seed=replicates[i].seed)` repeats it. `SimulationReplicates` (`py-commol/commol/api/results.py`) is a list of `SimulationResults`:

| Member                                        | Returns                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| --------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `replicates[i]`, `len(replicates)`            | One run, with its `seed`; the number of runs                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `seed`, `seeds`, `positions`                  | The seed the replicate seeds derive from, the seed of each replicate, the positions                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `mean()`                                      | `SimulationResults` of the mean of every output at each position                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `quantiles(levels)`                           | `{level: SimulationResults}`, at each position, by [the one quantile](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/codebase/decisions/results/#one-confidence-interval-convention) (NumPy's `method="hazen"`)                                              |
| `member_statistics(output, confidence_level)` | `mean`, `median`, `ci_lower`, `ci_upper`, `min`, `max` of one output at each position, reduced replicate by replicate with [the one quantile](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/codebase/decisions/results/#one-confidence-interval-convention) |

```python
from commol.api.plotter import SimulationPlotter

stochastic = Simulation(
    ModelBuilder(name="Stochastic Model")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_parameter(id="k", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k")
    .build(Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 1000, "B": 0}), engine="StochasticEvents")
)
replicates = stochastic.replicates(200, seed=42).run(num_steps=50)
mean = replicates.mean()
band = replicates.member_statistics("B", confidence_level=0.9)
SimulationPlotter(stochastic, replicates).plot_series()  # the mean and a 95 % band
print(replicates.seeds[:2] == [run.seed for run in replicates[:2]])  # True
```

The stochastic engines and what they draw are in [Stochastic Simulation](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/stochastic/index.md).

A run is reproducible from its model and its seed, on one platform and one commol version:

| Where                                     | The same seed gives                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The same machine and commol version       | The same run                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Another platform, the same commol version | The same random numbers (`Xoshiro256PlusPlus` and samplers written in commol, `crates/commol-random/`), but the rate functions (`exp`, `sin`, `log`, …) come from the system's math library, which can differ in the last bit between operating systems; a run there is equal in distribution and rarely differs draw by draw |
| Another commol version                    | A run that may change; the changelog says so                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

## Accumulators

An accumulator output starts at 0 and only grows: it is the total that its transitions have moved since step 0. Here `cum_ab` is everything that has moved from `A` to `B`, so `A` plus `cum_ab` stays at the initial `A`:

```python
print(round(results["A"][-1] + results["cum_ab"][-1]))  # 900
```

## Stratified outputs

With stratifications, every bin and accumulator has one output per combination of categories, named `{id}_{category}_{category}…` in the order the stratifications were declared.

```python
stratified = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Stratified")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    .add_stratification(id="type", categories=["t1", "t2"])
    .add_accumulator(id="cum_ab", name="Total moved from A to B")
    .add_parameter(id="k", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k", accumulators=["cum_ab"])
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 1000, "B": 0},
            stratification_fractions={
                "group": {"g1": 0.5, "g2": 0.5},
                "type": {"t1": 0.5, "t2": 0.5},
            },
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

stratified_simulation = Simulation(stratified)
stratified_results = stratified_simulation.run(num_steps=50)

print(stratified_simulation.outputs_for("B"))
# ['B_g1_t1', 'B_g1_t2', 'B_g2_t1', 'B_g2_t2']
print(stratified_simulation.group_outputs(["A", "cum_ab"])["cum_ab"])
# ['cum_ab_g1_t1', 'cum_ab_g1_t2', 'cum_ab_g2_t1', 'cum_ab_g2_t2']
```

### Totals by bin

`total_series` sums every output of the ids you give, at each position:

```python
total_b = stratified_simulation.total_series(stratified_results, ["B"])
total_ab = stratified_simulation.total_series(stratified_results, ["A", "B"])
print(round(total_ab[-1]))  # 1000: A and B hold the whole total
```

Do not select outputs by name prefix

`[k for k in results if k.startswith("B_")]` also matches an accumulator named `B_events`, and, with conditional stratifications, outputs may have fewer suffixes than their siblings. `outputs_for`, `group_outputs` and `total_series` use the model structure, so neither case can go wrong.

### Totals by category

To select compartments by category, use their labels from `model.structure.initial_state(model.process)`: each entry has `name`, `bin` and `categories`.

```python
in_g1 = [
    compartment.name
    for compartment in stratified.structure.initial_state(stratified.process)
    if compartment.categories.get("group") == "g1"
]
print(in_g1)  # ['A_g1_t1', 'A_g1_t2', 'B_g1_t1', 'B_g1_t2']

total_g1 = [
    sum(stratified_results[name][step] for name in in_g1)
    for step in range(len(stratified_results[in_g1[0]]))
]
print(round(total_g1[-1]))  # 500: g1 started with half of every bin
```

## Windowed totals

`windowed_totals` turns a cumulative output into the amount it gained in each window of length `window` on the axis. Window `w` covers `(w · window, (w + 1) · window]`, and each value is the output at the end of the window minus the output at its start. Both must be positions of the results.

```python
per_week = stratified_simulation.windowed_totals(
    stratified_results, ["cum_ab"], window=7
)
print(len(per_week))  # 7: the complete windows of a 50-step run
```

| Argument | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                           |
| -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ids`    | Accumulator ids; their outputs are summed first.                                                                                                                                  |
| `window` | The window length on the axis. Must be positive.                                                                                                                                  |
| `at`     | The positions where windows close. By default, every complete window of the results (`window_ends`). Pass observation positions to get the values a calibration compares against. |

The window grid and the same reduction work on any series with the module-level functions of `py-commol/commol/api/windows.py`:

| Function                                              | Returns                                                                                                                             |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `window_start(i, window)`, `window_end(i, window)`    | The positions that bound window `i`: `i · window` and `(i + 1) · window`                                                            |
| `window_index(at, window)`                            | The window that holds a position, `max(ceil(at / window) − 1, 0)`; the inverse of `window_end`. Reports place observations with it. |
| `window_ends(window, end)`                            | Every complete window end up to `end`                                                                                               |
| `windowed_totals(series, positions, window, at=None)` | The gain of a series over each window                                                                                               |

```python
from commol import window_end, window_ends, window_index, windowed_totals

print(window_ends(window=7, end=30))                       # [7, 14, 21, 28]
print(window_end(0, 7), window_index(7, 7), window_index(7.5, 7))  # 7 0 1
print(windowed_totals([0, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28], range(8), 3))  # [6, 15]
```

A window need not be a whole number of steps: see [Reporting at any position](#reporting-at-any-position).

## Differential equations

A model built with `engine="DifferentialEquations"` runs in continuous time. The engine (`crates/commol-differential/`) integrates `dX/dt = Σ flows(t, X)` with the ODE solver [diffsol](https://github.com/martinjrobins/diffsol). The flows are the same as in a difference model: the same transitions, rates, accumulators, outputs, calibration, reports and plots. Only the way the engine advances changes.

```python
import math

from commol import ODESolver

ode_model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Decay")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="B")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.1)
    .add_accumulator(id="moved", name="Moved from A to B")
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1", accumulators=["moved"])
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 1000, "B": 0},
        ),
        engine="DifferentialEquations",
        settings=ODESolver(method="tsit45", rtol=1e-8, atol=1e-8),
    )
)

ode = Simulation(ode_model)
at = ode.run_at([0, 0.5, 2.25])
print(round(at["A"][2], 3), round(1000 * math.exp(-0.1 * 2.25), 3))  # 798.516 798.516
print(round(ode.run(num_steps=10)["moved"][10], 1))  # 632.1: the integral of the flow
```

### Solver settings

`ODESolver` holds the settings of the `DifferentialEquations` engine. They are part of the model (`Model.engine.settings`), so a saved model reproduces its runs. Pass them where you choose the engine, `build(engine="DifferentialEquations", settings=...)`, so one builder can build the model for each engine with its own settings; without them the defaults apply. The `DifferenceEquations` engine takes no settings: the engine rejects settings of another engine with an error that names both (`ValidationError`).

| Field    | Default    | Meaning                                                                                                                                                     |
| -------- | ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `method` | `"tsit45"` | `"tsit45"`: explicit Runge–Kutta 5(4), for non-stiff models. `"bdf"`: backward differentiation formulas, for stiff models (rates of very different speeds). |
| `rtol`   | `1e-6`     | Relative tolerance of each state component.                                                                                                                 |
| `atol`   | `1e-6`     | Absolute tolerance of each state component, in the unit of the bins.                                                                                        |

`bdf` builds its Jacobian from a finite-difference Jacobian-vector product. It uses a dense matrix below `SPARSE_THRESHOLD` state components and a sparse one from there (`crates/commol-differential/src/solve.rs`).

A run stops with `RuntimeError` when the solver cannot take a step, or when a step leaves the state not finite, as when the solution blows up. The message names the last position the solver reached, with either method.

### Time inside a step

On `[n, n + 1)` a rate sees `step = n` and the position `t`, which moves continuously. A rate that reads `step`, a `"pulse"` series or a pulse pattern (`AxisPattern.pulse`, `pulses`, `periodic`) is constant on its unit interval, and the engine restarts the integration at each integer where such a rate can jump. A proportional pulse `p` on step `n` acts as the constant rate `p` for one unit: it moves `1 − e^(−p)` of its source, not `p` as in a difference model. To move a fraction at once, use an [impulse](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/transitions/#impulses).

A `"step_function"` or `"linear"` [series](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/building-models/#series-parameters) and the patterns `AxisPattern.interval` and `linear_ramp` read `t`, so they change at any position, and the engine restarts the integration at their points and bounds. In a difference model `t` equals `step`, so they give the same results as a rate that reads `step`.

A rate can also jump where `t` reaches a value that it compares `t` with, such as `if(t >= t_on, k1, 0)`. The engine restarts the integration there too, so the solver cannot step over a short window. This works when the value reads only numbers, `pi`, `e` and parameters with a constant or calibrated value, and `t` is one side of the comparison: write `t >= 10`, not `t - 10 >= 0`. A jump that depends on the state, such as `if(t >= A, ...)`, is not found.

A rate of a differential model is continuous, not a fraction per step; see [What a rate means](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/core-concepts/#what-a-rate-means). `Model.axis_units()` gives the rate that the engine of a model reads from a mean span or a probability over a period; see [Units of the axis](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/core-concepts/#units-of-the-axis).

```python
from commol import AxisPattern

pulse_model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Pulse")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="B")
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate=AxisPattern.pulse(at=2, value=0.2))
)
all_in_a = Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 1000, "B": 0})
ode_pulse = Simulation(
    pulse_model.build(all_in_a, engine="DifferentialEquations")
).run(num_steps=3)
print(round(ode_pulse["A"][2] - ode_pulse["A"][3], 1))  # 181.3 = 1000 (1 − e^−0.2)
```

### Reporting at any position

`run_at(at)` reports at sorted positions on the axis, from the dense output of the solver. Observations (`ObservedDataPoint.at`), windows (`ObservedDataPoint.window`) and constraint positions (`CalibrationConstraint.at`) may lie between integers for a differential model: the calibration reads the engine at those positions ([Observations](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-observations/#positions-between-integers)). A difference model reports only at integer steps; the engine rejects any other position and names the object that holds it.

Windows, reports and plots read a value at a position of the results, so a window of `2.5` works once the results hold its ends:

```python
ends = window_ends(window=2.5, end=10)    # [2.5, 5.0, 7.5, 10.0]
ode_windows = ode.run_at([0.0, *ends])
gained = ode.windowed_totals(ode_windows, ["moved"], window=2.5)
print([round(value, 1) for value in gained])  # [221.2, 172.3, 134.2, 104.5]
```

## Plotting

`SimulationPlotter(simulation, results)` draws one subplot per output with seaborn, and returns the matplotlib `Figure`. With the `SimulationReplicates` of a stochastic engine, `plot_series` draws their mean and a band of `confidence_level` (default 0.95), each replicate reduced to the plotted series first:

```python
from commol import PlotConfig, SimulationPlotter

plotter = SimulationPlotter(simulation, results)  # the results of the first run
plotter.plot_series(output_file="series.png")
plotter.plot_cumulative(output_file="cumulative.png")

plotter.plot_series(
    output_file="custom.png",
    config=PlotConfig(figsize=(16, 10), dpi=150, style="whitegrid", palette="Set2", context="talk"),
    series=["B", "C"],
    x_label="Week",
    tick_every=10,
    position_label=lambda at: f"w{int(at) // 7}",
    linewidth=2.5,
    alpha=0.8,
)
```

| Argument                                  | Default                                        | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `output_file`                             | `None`                                         | Where to save the figure. `None` only returns it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `series`                                  | `None` (every output)                          | What to plot, one subplot each: an output name (`B_g1`) or a bin or accumulator id (`B`), which plots the sum of its outputs (`Simulation.outputs_for`). An exact output name wins. An unknown entry raises `ValueError`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `observed_data`                           | `None`                                         | `ObservedDataPoint`s to draw on the subplot of their `label`, at their positions (a differential model may observe between integers). When the observations of a series share one sum of outputs and one factor and have no window, the model line covers every position of the results. Otherwise the line joins the model value of each observation at its position, read through its own outputs, `window` and factor as the loss reads it (`ValueError` when the results have no value at a position or a window start). |
| `calibration_result`                      | `None`                                         | A `CalibrationResult` gives the factor values that scale the model. A [`Predictive`](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/#the-predictive) draws the weighted median of its draws and their band of `confidence_level`, each draw read through the observation operator (sums, windows, factors), at the position of each observation when the line of `observed_data` is.                                                                                                                                |
| `prediction_intervals`                    | `None`                                         | `plot_series` only. The `PredictionIntervals` of a [conformal method](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/conformal/index.md): the subplot of each of their series, by label, shows the band from `lower` to `upper` and the point prediction, dashed. An unbounded interval is left out of the band.                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `config`                                  | `PlotConfig()`                                 | Figure size, dpi, layout and seaborn style.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `show_legend`                             | `True`                                         | `plot_series` only.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `x_label`, `tick_every`, `position_label` | `"Step"`, every plotted position, the position | `plot_series` only. Label the x axis, for example in weeks. The x axis shows `results.positions`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| other keyword arguments                   | —                                              | Passed to `seaborn.lineplot`, such as `linewidth` or `alpha`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

| `PlotConfig` field | Default            | Values                                                      |
| ------------------ | ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `figsize`          | `(12, 8)`          | Inches (width, height)                                      |
| `dpi`              | `100`              | Resolution                                                  |
| `layout`           | `None` (automatic) | `(rows, columns)`                                           |
| `style`            | `None`             | `"darkgrid"`, `"whitegrid"`, `"dark"`, `"white"`, `"ticks"` |
| `palette`          | `None`             | A seaborn palette or matplotlib colormap, such as `"Set2"`  |
| `context`          | `None`             | `"paper"`, `"notebook"`, `"talk"`, `"poster"`               |

`style`, `palette` and `context` apply to the figure of one plot only. Each method of `SimulationPlotter` draws in a copy of `matplotlib.rcParams` (`_scoped_style` in `py-commol/commol/api/plotter.py`), so the figures that you draw with matplotlib after a plot of commol keep your own style.

To compare with observations:

```python
from commol import ObservedDataPoint

observed = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=10, output="B", value=45.2),
    ObservedDataPoint(at=20, output="B", value=78.5),
]
plotter.plot_series(output_file="with_data.png", observed_data=observed)
```

# Stochastic Simulation

[Back to Home](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/index.md)

A stochastic engine runs the process of a model as whole units that move at random, with no change to the process: the rates of the model become the probabilities or the hazards of its events. Use it when the variability between runs, an extinction or the behaviour of small amounts matters. This page covers the two stochastic engines of an aggregate model, how a rate becomes an event, whole units, the methods and their cost, and calibration with replicates.

## Quick path

```python
from commol import Aggregate, ModelBuilder, Simulation

builder = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Stochastic Model")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
)
structure = Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 999, "B": 1, "C": 0})

model = builder.build(structure, engine="StochasticEvents")
simulation = Simulation(model)

one_run = simulation.run(num_steps=100, seed=1)
print(one_run["C"][-1] == int(one_run["C"][-1]))  # True: whole units

replicates = simulation.replicates(100, seed=2).run(num_steps=100)
print(len(replicates))  # 100 runs, one seed each
died_out = sum(run["C"][-1] < 10 for run in replicates)
print(died_out)  # about a third of the runs: the one unit of B leaves before it spreads
```

The same `builder` and `structure` build the deterministic model with `engine="DifferentialEquations"`: only the engine changes.

## When to use it

| You need                                                            | Engine                                           |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| The mean behaviour of a large amount                                | `DifferentialEquations` or `DifferenceEquations` |
| How much runs vary, and the spread of an output                     | `StochasticEvents` or `StochasticSteps`          |
| The chance that an amount reaches zero and stays there (extinction) | `StochasticEvents` or `StochasticSteps`          |
| Small amounts, where a unit more or less changes the outcome        | `StochasticEvents` or `StochasticSteps`          |

## The two engines

| Engine             | Time           | Method                                                                               | Rate meaning                                | Positions                         | Crate               |
| ------------------ | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| `StochasticEvents` | Continuous     | Gillespie's direct method (the stochastic simulation algorithm, SSA), or tau-leaping | `continuous`: a hazard per unit of the axis | Any finite, non-negative position | `commol-stochastic` |
| `StochasticSteps`  | Discrete steps | The chain binomial                                                                   | `per_step`: a probability per step          | Integer steps                     | `commol-stochastic` |

Their mean-field limits are the deterministic engines: the expected change of the state of `StochasticEvents` is the right-hand side of `DifferentialEquations`, and the expected step of `StochasticSteps` is the step of `DifferenceEquations` while no cap acts (see below). A rate keeps its meaning: a `per_step` rate of a difference model is the probability of the chain binomial, and a `continuous` rate of a differential model is the hazard of the events ([What a rate means](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/core-concepts/#what-a-rate-means)).

## How a rate becomes an event

Each flow of the model is one kind of event. An event moves one unit: it takes one from each source of the flow, and adds one to each target and to each accumulator that counts the flow (`CompiledModel::flow_changes` in `crates/commol-model/src/system.rs`).

| Rate                    | `StochasticEvents` (propensity)                                       | `StochasticSteps` (draw of a step)                           |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Proportional, `k`       | Each unit of the source leaves at hazard `k`: propensity `k × source` | Each unit leaves with probability `k`: `Binomial(source, k)` |
| Absolute, `r`           | Events at rate `r`                                                    | `Poisson(r)`, capped by what the sources still hold          |
| No source (inflow), `r` | Events at rate `r`                                                    | `Poisson(r)`                                                 |

- `StochasticEvents`: a flow has no events while a source holds fewer units than an event takes. A negative propensity is an error that names the flow.
- `StochasticSteps`: every draw reads the state at the start of the step. The units of one compartment leave by its proportional flows in one multinomial draw (each flow with its probability, staying with `1 − Σ k`), so a unit never leaves twice and an amount never goes below zero. The absolute flows then draw in the order of the model, each capped by what its sources still hold. A negative rate, a proportional rate above 1, or proportional rates out of one compartment that sum to more than 1 raise `InfeasibleStateError`, which names the compartment, the step and the flows (`StochasticSteps::step` in `crates/commol-stochastic/src/steps.rs`).

```python
from commol import InfeasibleStateError

too_likely = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Too likely")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.7)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.5)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1")
    .add_transition(id="t_ac", source=["A"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
    .build(structure, engine="StochasticSteps")
)
try:
    Simulation(too_likely).run(num_steps=5, seed=1)
except InfeasibleStateError as error:
    print(error)  # At step 0, the proportional rates out of compartment 'A': flows 't_ab' 0.7, 't_ac' 0.5 sum to 1.2, above 1. ...
```

`Model.describe()` shows the events in its `dynamics` section: one row per flow with its change of the state and its propensity or its draw ([Describing a Model](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/describing-models/index.md)):

```python
print(model.describe().render("markdown").split("### Events")[1].split("\n\n")[1])
# | Transition | Change | Propensity |
# |---|---|---|
# | t_ab | A -1, B +1 | k1 * A * B / total |
# | t_bc | B -1, C +1 | k2 * B |
```

## Whole units

A stochastic engine moves whole units, so it starts from whole amounts (`check_model` in `crates/commol-model/src/builder.rs`):

| Initial amounts                           | What happens                                                                                             |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The amount of a bin is not a whole number | `build` raises `ValueError` and names the engine and the bin                                             |
| Every amount is whole                     | Nothing more is needed                                                                                   |
| An amount is not whole                    | `build` raises `ValueError`, unless the settings of the engine name a `rounding`; the message lists both |

There is no default rounding: with small amounts the rounding decides which compartments start with a unit, so it is a modelling choice. Half a unit in each of ten groups starts five groups with one unit and five with none.

| `rounding`            | Start of each run                                                                                                                                                   |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"largest_remainder"` | The same whole amounts in every run: in each bin, each amount rounded down, and the units left over to the largest remainders, so they sum to the amount of the bin |
| `"random"`            | A multinomial draw of the amount of each bin with the fractions of the model, in each run, so the mean start equals the amounts of the model                        |

Both round each bin on its own, so a unit never moves to another bin, such as from a bin of a concentration to a bin of a count.

```python
from commol import StochasticEventsSettings

groups = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Groups")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=[f"g{i}" for i in range(10)])
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * B / total")
)
seeded = Aggregate(
    bin_amounts={"A": 995, "B": 5},
    stratification_fractions={"group": {f"g{i}": 0.1 for i in range(10)}},
)
try:
    groups.build(seeded, engine="StochasticEvents")
except ValueError as error:
    print("largest_remainder" in str(error), "random" in str(error))  # True True

grouped = groups.build(
    seeded,
    engine="StochasticEvents",
    settings=StochasticEventsSettings(rounding="random"),
)
start = Simulation(grouped).run_at([0.0], seed=3)
print(sum(start[f"B_g{i}"][0] for i in range(10)) + sum(start[f"A_g{i}"][0] for i in range(10)))
# 1000.0
```

Initial conditions that calibration sets go through the same rounding. With no rounding, a calibrated value that is not whole is an error that lists the two options.

## Seeds and replicates

A run is reproducible from its model and its seed: `simulation.run(…, seed=s)` gives one run, and `simulation.replicates(n, seed=s).run(…)` gives `n` runs with one seed each, in parallel. A run does not depend on the positions it reports at: the output at a position is the state after the last event before it. See [Randomness, seeds and replicates](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/simulations/#randomness-seeds-and-replicates) for the seeds, `SimulationReplicates` and its statistics, plots of the mean and a band, and reports.

```python
again = simulation.run(num_steps=100, seed=1)
print(again == one_run)  # True
print(replicates.member_statistics("C", confidence_level=0.9)["ci_lower"][-1] >= 0)  # True
```

## Methods and their cost

`StochasticEvents` takes `StochasticEventsSettings`, and `StochasticSteps` takes `StochasticStepsSettings` (only `rounding`):

| Setting     | Default    | Meaning                                                                                                                      |
| ----------- | ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `method`    | `"direct"` | `"direct"`: one event at a time, exact. `"tau_leaping"`: a Poisson number of events of each flow in a leap, an approximation |
| `tau`       | `None`     | The length of a leap of `"tau_leaping"`; `None` chooses each leap as Cao, Gillespie and Petzold (2006) do                    |
| `epsilon`   | `0.03`     | How much a propensity may change in a chosen leap, relative to its value                                                     |
| `tolerance` | `1e-8`     | Relative tolerance of the time of an event when a rate reads `t`                                                             |
| `rounding`  | `None`     | See [Whole units](#whole-units)                                                                                              |

- **Cost of the direct method.** The number of events grows with the total and with the rates: every unit that moves is one event. For a large total, use `"tau_leaping"` or a deterministic engine.
- **Tau-leaping.** A chosen leap is as long as the propensities allow while they change by less than `epsilon`; a leap that would hold fewer than ten events is one exact event instead, and a leap that leaves an amount below zero is halved and drawn again. A fixed `tau` is first-order accurate: a smaller `tau` is closer to the direct method.
- **Rates that read `t`.** Between events the state is fixed, but a rate that reads `t`, such as `k * (1 + sin(t))`, still changes. The direct method then integrates the total propensity from the last event until it reaches an exponential draw (a time change, Anderson 2007), within `tolerance`. A model whose rates do not read `t` pays nothing for it.
- **Breakpoints.** The engine stops at every position where a rate can jump (the impulses, the values a rate compares `t` with, the points of a series read at `t`, and every integer when a rate reads `step`), so no wait and no leap crosses one (`CompiledModel::breakpoints`).
- **Impulses.** At its positions, before the events there, a proportional impulse moves a binomial draw of its source (its rate is the probability that one unit moves, between 0 and 1); an absolute impulse moves its rate, a whole number of units. Each moves at most what its sources still hold.

```python
leaping = builder.build(
    structure,
    engine="StochasticEvents",
    settings=StochasticEventsSettings(method="tau_leaping"),
)
leaped = Simulation(leaping).replicates(100, seed=2).run(num_steps=100)
print(abs(leaped.mean()["C"][-1] - replicates.mean()["C"][-1]) < 150)  # True
```

## Calibration with replicates

A calibration of a stochastic model runs `replicates` runs per evaluation with common random numbers, and compares the observations with the summary of the replicates you choose: `"mean"`, `"median"`, `Quantile(q)` or `"crps"` ([Stochastic engines](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration/#stochastic-engines)).

```python
from commol import (
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
)

mean = replicates.mean()
observed = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=at, output="C", value=mean["C"][at]) for at in (40, 70, 100)
]
unknown = builder.build(structure, engine="StochasticEvents")
unknown.update_parameters({"k2": None})
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observed,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k2", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.01, max_bound=0.5)
    ],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=100),
    replicates=50,
    replicate_summary="mean",
    seed=7,
)
result = Calibrator(Simulation(unknown), problem).run()
print(0.05 < result.best_parameters["k2"] < 0.2)  # True: near 0.1
```

## Checklist

- [ ] The engine is `StochasticEvents` (continuous time) or `StochasticSteps` (per-step probabilities), as the rates of the model mean.
- [ ] The amount of each bin is whole, and the settings name a `rounding` when the amount of a compartment is not.
- [ ] Every run has a seed, or keeps the one commol drew (`results.seed`).
- [ ] A large total uses `"tau_leaping"` or a deterministic engine.
- [ ] A calibration sets `replicates`, `replicate_summary` and `seed`.

# Model Calibration

[Back to Home](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/index.md)

Calibration finds the parameter values (and, if you want, initial conditions and observation scale factors) that make a model reproduce observed data. You describe the observations and the unknowns in a `CalibrationProblem`, and a `Calibrator` runs an optimizer in the Rust engine.

| Topic                                                              | Page                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The workflow, the problem, losses and results                      | This page                                                                                                             |
| Maximum likelihood with a model of the noise of each series        | [Observation Models](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/observation-models/index.md)             |
| Calibrating initial conditions                                     | [Calibrating Initial Conditions](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-initial-conditions/index.md) |
| Several outputs, aggregates, weights, scale factors, windowed data | [Observations](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-observations/index.md)                         |
| Nelder-Mead and particle swarm settings                            | [Optimizers](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-optimizers/index.md)                             |
| Relations the result must respect                                  | [Constraints](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-constraints/index.md)                           |
| Reports of a calibrated model and run                              | [Reports](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/reports/index.md)                                               |
| Samples, predictive bands and scores                               | [Uncertainty](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/index.md)                                       |

## Quick path

```python
from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    Simulation,
)

def basic_model(k1: float | None, k2: float | None, engine="DifferenceEquations"):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Basic Model")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=k2)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .build(
            Aggregate(
                bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0},
            ),
            engine=engine,
        )
    )

# Observations generated from k1 = 0.4, k2 = 0.1
truth = Simulation(basic_model(0.4, 0.1)).run(num_steps=50)
observed_data = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=truth["B"][step])
    for step in range(5, 51, 5)
]

# 1. A model whose unknowns are None
model = basic_model(None, None)

# 2. The problem: observations, unknowns, loss and optimizer
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observed_data,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
        CalibrationParameter(id="k2", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
    ],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000),
    seed=42,
)

# 3. Calibrate
result = Calibrator(Simulation(model), problem).run()
print({name: round(value, 3) for name, value in sorted(result.best_parameters.items())})
# {'k1': 0.4, 'k2': 0.1}

# 4. Write the values back, and simulate
model.apply_calibration_parameters(result, problem)
calibrated = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=100)
```

A `Simulation` follows its model: after `apply_calibration_parameters` or `update_parameters`, its next `run` (and its `engine`) uses the new values, also when it was created while a parameter was `None`. See [Simulations](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/simulations/#simulation).

## The problem

| `CalibrationProblem` field    | Type                                        | Default  | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `observed_data`               | `list[ObservedDataPoint]`                   | required | What the model must reproduce. See [Observations](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-observations/index.md).                                                                                     |
| `parameters`                  | `list[CalibrationParameter]`                | required | The unknowns and their bounds.                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `loss_function`               | `str \| None`                               | `None`   | How the misfit is measured; see [Losses](#losses). A problem has `loss_function` or `observation_models`, exactly one.                                                                                                |
| `observation_models`          | `dict[str, ObservationModel] \| None`       | `None`   | One observation model per series label: the fit maximizes their likelihood. See [Observation Models](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/observation-models/index.md).                            |
| `optimization_config`         | `NelderMeadConfig` or `ParticleSwarmConfig` | required | The optimizer and its settings. See [Optimizers](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-optimizers/index.md).                                                                                        |
| `constraints`                 | `list[CalibrationConstraint]`               | `[]`     | Relations the result must respect. See [Constraints](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-constraints/index.md).                                                                                   |
| `normalize_observations`      | `bool`                                      | `False`  | Divides each residual by the RMS of its observation series, so series of very different size weigh the same. Needs a loss.                                                                                            |
| `initial_condition_remainder` | `str \| None`                               | `None`   | The compartment or bin that absorbs the difference when initial conditions are calibrated. See [Calibrating Initial Conditions](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-initial-conditions/index.md). |
| `seed`                        | `int \| None`                               | `None`   | Makes every random choice reproducible.                                                                                                                                                                               |

### Observations

| `ObservedDataPoint` field | Type                | Default  | Meaning                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------- | ------------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `at`                      | `float`             | required | The position of the observation on the axis. A difference model accepts integer steps only.                      |
| `output`                  | `str \| None`       | `None`   | The output it observes: a compartment or accumulator name, such as `B` or `B_g1`. Give `output` or `outputs`.    |
| `outputs`                 | `list[str] \| None` | `None`   | Outputs to sum before the comparison; needs a `label`.                                                           |
| `label`                   | `str`               | `output` | The name of the observed series in reports, plots and the normalization.                                         |
| `value`                   | `float`             | required | The observed value.                                                                                              |
| `weight`                  | `float`             | `1.0`    | How much the observation counts in every loss, and the power of its term of a likelihood; see [Losses](#losses). |
| `factor_id`               | `str \| None`       | `None`   | A `factor` parameter that multiplies the prediction.                                                             |
| `window`                  | `float \| None`     | `None`   | Compares with the gain over `(at − window, at]` instead of the value.                                            |
| `trials`                  | `int \| None`       | `None`   | The trials of the observation, for a `BinomialObservations()` model that reads them from each observation.       |

### Unknowns

| `CalibrationParameter` field | Type            | Default  | Meaning                                                           |
| ---------------------------- | --------------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `id`                         | `str`           | required | What to calibrate; depends on `parameter_type`.                   |
| `parameter_type`             | `str`           | required | `"parameter"`, `"initial_condition"`, `"factor"` or `"noise"`.    |
| `min_bound`, `max_bound`     | `float`         | required | The search interval.                                              |
| `initial_guess`              | `float \| None` | `None`   | Where the optimizer starts; the midpoint of the bounds if `None`. |

| `parameter_type`      | `id` names                                                                                                                                | The value is                                                                                                                                                                            |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"parameter"`         | A model parameter, usually declared with `value=None`                                                                                     | The parameter value                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `"initial_condition"` | A bin, a category, or an expanded compartment                                                                                             | An amount in the unit of its bin, or the split of a category; see [Calibrating Initial Conditions](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-initial-conditions/index.md) |
| `"factor"`            | Any new id, used by observations through `factor_id`                                                                                      | A factor on the predictions; not part of the model                                                                                                                                      |
| `"noise"`             | Any new id, named by an [observation model](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/observation-models/#noise-parameters) | An argument of the model, such as its standard deviation; not part of the model                                                                                                         |

`"parameter"`, `"factor"` and `"noise"` work with every kind of model. The other types are values of the model kind, and the kind declares which it accepts (`model.structure.calibration_value_types()`): an aggregate model accepts `"initial_condition"`. A type the kind does not accept raises a `ValueError` that names the kind when you create the `Calibrator`.

## Losses

A problem has a loss or observation models, exactly one, and neither has a default: what to fit is a modelling choice. A loss measures the residuals; [observation models](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/observation-models/index.md) say how each series scatters, and the fit maximizes their likelihood, so its loss is `−log L`. `CalibrationProblem` raises a `ValueError` with both or neither.

| `loss_function` | Formula (residual `r = observed − predicted`, weight `w`) | Use when                              |
| --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `"sse"`         | `Σ w·r²`                                                  | The usual choice                      |
| `"rmse"`        | `√(Σ w·r² / Σ w)`                                         | You want the error in the data's unit |
| `"mae"`         | \`Σ w·                                                    | r                                     |

How weights count

Every loss uses a weight the same way: `weight=2.0` makes an observation count twice as much as one with weight 1.0. With every weight at its default of 1.0, the losses are the plain sum of squares, root mean square and mean absolute error. `LossConfig` in `crates/commol-calibration/src/types.rs` computes them; the discrepancy (`crates/commol-calibration/src/discrepancy.rs`) applies them.

With `normalize_observations=True`, each residual is first divided by the RMS of the observations of its series (its `label`).

A run the model does not allow gets a penalty instead of a loss: a run with values that are not finite, or a difference step that leaves an amount below zero (`InfeasibleStateError`, see [Amounts below zero](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/transitions/#amounts-below-zero)). The penalty is much larger than any fit, and the run is not recorded in the history, so the optimizer moves away from it and goes on. Any other error of a run, such as a rate that cannot be evaluated or that is not a number, stops the calibration with its message (`OptimizationObjective` in `crates/commol-calibration/src/objective.rs`, the only place that turns an infeasible point into a penalty).

## Stochastic engines

With a stochastic engine, one run per evaluation would make the loss change from one evaluation to the next for the same parameters, and Nelder-Mead and particle swarm would chase the noise. So each evaluation runs `replicates` replicates with **common random numbers**: the same replicate seeds at every evaluation, derived from `seed`. The loss is then a deterministic function of the parameters (`CalibrationProblem::with_replicates` in `crates/commol-calibration/src/calibration_problem.rs`).

You choose what each observation is compared with; there is no default, because what to fit is a modelling choice:

| `replicate_summary` | Compared with each observation               | Loss                                         |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `"mean"`            | The mean of the replicates                   | `loss_function`                              |
| `"median"`          | The median                                   | `loss_function`                              |
| `Quantile(q)`       | The quantile `q`                             | `loss_function`                              |
| `"crps"`            | The empirical distribution of the replicates | The continuous ranked probability score, \`E |

```python
stochastic = basic_model(None, 0.1, engine="StochasticSteps")
runs = Simulation(basic_model(0.4, 0.1)).run(num_steps=50)
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=[
        ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=runs["B"][step])
        for step in range(5, 51, 5)
    ],
    parameters=[CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0)],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=200),
    replicates=50,
    replicate_summary="crps",  # or "mean", "median", Quantile(0.9)
    seed=7,
)
result = Calibrator(Simulation(stochastic), problem).run()
print(round(result.best_parameters["k1"], 1))  # 0.4
```

| Rule                                                                                                                                         | Where                                                                                   |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A stochastic engine needs `replicates`, `replicate_summary` and `seed`; without one, `Calibrator` raises and the message lists the summaries | `rust_loss_config` in `py-commol/commol/context/_model/engine_state.py`                 |
| A deterministic engine does not use `replicates` and `replicate_summary`                                                                     | The same                                                                                |
| A stochastic engine needs a loss: with `observation_models`, `Calibrator` raises a `ValueError`                                              | `PyCalibrationProblem::new` in `py-commol/src/inference.rs`; `Discrepancy::set_summary` |
| The summaries and the CRPS are computed in `LossConfig`, and the observation weights apply to every option                                   | `LossConfig::replicate_loss` in `crates/commol-calibration/src/types.rs`                |
| A constraint at positions is checked on every replicate                                                                                      | `CalibrationProblem::evaluate`                                                          |

With one replicate the CRPS is the absolute error. The [predictive](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/#the-predictive) of a sample runs every replicate of each draw.

## Results

`Calibrator(simulation, problem)` checks the problem against the model, and `run()` returns a `CalibrationResult`:

| `CalibrationResult` field | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `best_parameters`         | `dict[str, float]`: the best value of every unknown, in the order of `problem.parameters`                                                                                                                                                          |
| `final_loss`              | The loss at `best_parameters`; with observation models, the negative log-likelihood                                                                                                                                                                |
| `iterations`              | The optimizer iterations performed                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `converged`               | `True` only when the optimizer met its convergence test or `target_cost`; a run that used all `max_iterations` is `False`. See [Optimizers](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-optimizers/#converged-and-termination_reason). |
| `termination_reason`      | Why it stopped                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `starts`, `failed_runs`   | Every start that finished, and why each failed one did. See [Several starts](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-optimizers/#several-starts).                                                                                  |

```python
print(result.converged, result.termination_reason)
print(f"loss = {result.final_loss:.3g} after {result.iterations} iterations")
```

| `Calibrator` member                                     | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `run(starts=1)`                                         | Runs the optimizer from `starts` start points and returns the best `CalibrationResult`. See [Several starts](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-optimizers/#several-starts). |
| `run_with_history()`                                    | Returns a `CalibrationHistory`: the result and every evaluation of a feasible point.                                                                                                              |
| `uncertainty(method)`                                   | Runs an uncertainty method. See [Uncertainty](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/#the-entry-point).                                                                          |
| `num_observations`, `num_parameters`, `parameter_names` | Facts about the problem.                                                                                                                                                                          |

## Writing the result back

`Model.apply_calibration_parameters(result, problem)` writes every calibrated value into the model, routed by its `parameter_type`:

| `parameter_type`      | Written to                                                                           |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `"parameter"`         | The model parameter with that id                                                     |
| `"initial_condition"` | The initial conditions, so the model rebuilds exactly the state the optimizer scored |
| `"factor"`, `"noise"` | Nothing: they describe the observations, not the model                               |

It accepts a `CalibrationResult` or a plain `{id: value}` mapping, such as one of `sample.draws()`; a `ParameterSample` has no single set of values and raises `TypeError`. It computes the new definition first, so a rejected value leaves the model unchanged. To set values by hand, use `Model.update_parameters({...})`.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every unknown is `None` in the model and has a `CalibrationParameter`.
- [ ] Every observation names an output of the model (`Simulation.simulation_outputs`).
- [ ] The bounds are realistic, and the result is not stuck at a bound.
- [ ] `result.converged` is `True`, or you know why not.
- [ ] You simulate the calibrated model with a **new** `Simulation`.

| Fitting several or partial observations | [Observations](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-observations/index.md)                         |
